beats.title: Set the alternate interior angle to prove m ∥ n
beats.instruction: Two lines m and n are cut by transversal t. Drag point G to set the alternate interior angle ∠EFG to 90°. When ∠EFG equals the alternate interior angle at E (also 90°), the lines are parallel by the Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem.
beats.successMessage: ∠EFG = 90° = the alternate interior angle at E — Converse of the AIA Theorem proves m ∥ n.

beats.title: Two-column proof: proving m ∥ n from congruent alternate interior angles

steps.text: Given: ∠AEF ≅ ∠EFD. These two angles are alternate interior angles formed by transversal t cutting lines m and n between intersection points E (on m) and F (on n).
Statement: ∠AEF ≅ ∠EFD. Reason: Given. The congruence marks on the diagram confirm these angles are equal in measure.
Statement: m ∥ n. Reason: Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem — if two lines are cut by a transversal so that alternate interior angles are congruent, then the lines are parallel.

Verification: corresponding angles ∠AEB (upper-right at E) and ∠EFG (upper-right at F) are also congruent — a second check that m ∥ n. Co-interior angles ∠BEF and ∠EFD sum to 180°, a third confirmation.

items.prompt: Two lines are cut by a transversal. You measure the corresponding angles and find them equal. Which theorem proves the lines are parallel?
choices: Corresponding Angles Theorem
Converse of the Corresponding Angles Theorem
Alternate Interior Angles Theorem
Co-interior Angles Theorem
items.explanation: The Corresponding Angles Theorem says parallel lines produce equal corresponding angles. Its converse says equal corresponding angles prove the lines are parallel.

items.prompt: To use the Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem to prove two lines parallel, you must first establish that…
choices: the lines are in the same plane.
alternate interior angles are congruent.
co-interior angles are supplementary.
corresponding angles are supplementary.
items.explanation: The Converse of the AIA Theorem requires alternate interior angles to be congruent. Co-interior supplementary angles use the Converse of the Co-interior Angles Theorem instead.

items.prompt: Lines j and k are cut by a transversal. The alternate exterior angles are congruent. Which theorem proves j ∥ k?
choices: Converse of the Corresponding Angles Theorem
Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem
Converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem
Converse of the Co-interior Angles Theorem
hints: The given information is about alternate exterior angles — angles on opposite sides of the transversal, outside the two lines.
Each converse theorem matches its angle type: alternate exterior angles → Converse of AEA Theorem.
Converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem applies here.

items.prompt: Lines p and q are cut by a transversal. A pair of corresponding angles measures (4x + 10)° and (6x − 8)°. Find the value of x that makes p ∥ q.
hints: For corresponding angles to prove lines parallel, they must be congruent — set them equal.
18 = 2x, so x = 9. Check: both angles equal 46°.

items.prompt: Lines r and s are cut by a transversal. A pair of co-interior (same-side interior) angles measures (3x + 15)° and (5x + 13)°. Find the value of x that makes r ∥ s.
hints: For co-interior angles to prove lines parallel, they must be supplementary — they sum to 180°.

choices: Alternate Interior Angles Theorem

testItems.prompt: Which converse theorem uses co-interior (same-side interior) angles to prove lines parallel?
choices: Converse of the Corresponding Angles Theorem
Converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem
Converse of the Co-interior Angles Theorem
Converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem

testItems.prompt: Lines a and b are cut by a transversal. Alternate interior angles measure (5x − 3)° and (3x + 17)°. Find x so that a ∥ b.
The Alternate Interior Angles Theorem states: if lines are parallel, then alternate interior angles are congruent. Its logically equivalent contrapositive states…
choices: If lines are not parallel, then alternate interior angles are not congruent.
If alternate interior angles are congruent, then lines are parallel.
If alternate interior angles are not congruent, then lines are not parallel.
If lines are not parallel, then alternate interior angles are congruent.
testItems.explanation: The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is 'if not Q then not P,' which is logically equivalent to the original. The converse ('if Q then P') is a separate, independent theorem.

testItems.prompt: Lines c and d are cut by a transversal. Co-interior angles measure (7x + 4)° and (3x + 16)°. Find x so that c ∥ d.
testItems.explanation: Co-interior angles must be supplementary: (7x+4)+(3x+16)=180 → 10x+20=180 → 10x=160 → x=16. Angles: 116° and 64°; sum = 180° ✓.

testItems.prompt: A student says: 'I know m∥n because I measured one angle at each intersection and they look about equal.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: Nothing — visual inspection is sufficient for a proof.
The student needs to identify which angle relationship (corresponding, alternate interior, etc.) and verify the exact congruence condition for that relationship.
You need to measure all eight angles, not just two.
Visual inspection is fine as long as you use a protractor.
testItems.explanation: Proofs require stating the specific theorem used and showing the exact condition is met — just 'looking equal' does not constitute a valid geometric proof.
